newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi parties look to talks, killings reported.
newsitem.headline: Burundi parties look to talks, killings reported.

text.p: Officials said on Tuesday most of Burundi's factions had invitations to peace talks this month amid reports Hutu rebels killed hundreds of Hutu civilians in the northwest.

Burundi's Minister of Institutional Reform Eugene Nindorera said five groups had been invited including the government, the national assembly, its main parties and the main Hutu rebel group the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD).
The talks from August 25 in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha will be chaired by Julius Nyerere, the internationally-backed mediator on Burundi and Tanzania's former president.
But a diplomat said he was concerned Leonce Ngendakumana, the Hutu national assembly speaker seen by Nyerere as a key participant at the talks, might not be able to attend the Arusha meeting.
"Whether or not he can go, this is the key question," said the diplomat, adding the talks might not go ahead without him.

Ngendakumana is banned from leaving the country because justice ministry officials say he and other members of the Hutu-dominated Frodebu party are being investigated for their alleged involvement in massacres of Tutsis in 1993.

Burundi's independent radio production house Studio Ijambo on Tuesday quoted residents of the northwestern provinces of Cibitoke and Bubanza as saying more than 600 Hutu civilians were killed by rival Hutu rebels in the second half of July.

The residents, who had since fled, said the civilians were killed in fighting between the Hutu National Liberation Front (FNL) and the Forces for the Defence of Democracy, the armed wing of CNDD led by former interior minister Leonard Nyangoma.

They said the FNL accused the FDD of collaborating with Burundi's Tutsi military ruler Pierre Buyoya because the CNDD had agreed to peace talks with his military government, which seized power a year ago.
Nindorera said the government would ask for a total end to a regional embargo of Burundi and try to negotiate a ceasefire at the talks. The rebel groups have repeatedly refused to agree to any truce.

More than 250,000 people have been killed in Burundi in massacres and civil war between the Tutsi-dominated army and Hutu rebels since the assassination of Burundi's first Hutu president in October 1993.
